turn_text: Agriculture has always been a top priority for me. I've been very privileged to serve on the House Ag Committee and the Senate Ag Committee, and I feel very privileged now to be chairman of the Senate Agriculture Committee. Plus, if you do a good job while you represent the finest folks our country has to offer.
Evaluate the 14 farm bill, especially now as we are facing implementation. Is it what you hoped it would be?

Well, personally, I have some problems with the bill with regards to policy concerns. I'm somewhat worried and concerned that some of the subsidy levels and the way this is headed to farmers will be planning for the government as opposed to the market. That was the whole idea of the bill back in 1996 to move away from that and to emphasize such things as crop insurance. In the end result in 2014, we save and improve crop insurance. We're happy about that. We're too happy about the direction of the bill policy-wise.
Do you think with this legislation that you would have worked harder to get it than you will to keep it?

Well, that's a good question. It took us 400 days to get what we had and Finally, the issue of predictability and having a bill top any other issue with regards to changing it. If you spent 400 days with our producers out there wondering when on earth they're going to get a bill, not to mention their ag lenders, why we had to get a bill done. So getting it done, I think, was the primary issue. Now, there are those that say this will be the last farm bill. I don't think that's correct. I think we will always play a very important part in the economy of the United States. And we have always had several generations who didn't really appreciate where their food comes from. And now there's a whole generation who are very particular about their food and what they eat. So I think that interest will continue. We just have to keep up with our education efforts to try to make them understand that we need a reasonable agricultural policy.
Senator, where are the attackers and where are likely to be the challenges that would come after this policy either to take money away or to reopen and rewrite?

Well, Jeff, you always have during the ag appropriations bill. Of course, we haven't done it. Appropriation bills. We haven't done a budget in the Senate for seven years. If you can get budgets, well, then you get your reconciliation. Now I know I'm talking, you know, Washington talk here, but that allows you to do the spending bills. And then you have an ag spending bill, if you will, or an appropriation bill. You always have those who will take a particular interest in a particular program and try to cut it. You have those who I usually go to and say, look, if you want to run the Ag Committee, why don't you get on it? On the attackers, it usually comes from people who would like to cut spending and obviously we have a budget and the budget process is about to begin. There are many steps before we know if the Agriculture Committee must find savings within our jurisdiction over mandatory spending. We have risen to the challenge to find savings before. My goodness with an eighteen trillion dollar debt we have to really step up to that we can do it again if need to But I think any discussion over a particular part of the budget I think that's premature

turn_text: When we look to issues for 2015 and beyond agriculture it would really love to see and small business would love to see tax reform. Is that high enough on the agenda that can be accomplished in this 2015 or is that too close to the election?

Well we had hoped again that there was an area where we could work with the administration on comprehensive tax reform. Now that's the whole deal. If you stacked up the entire A tax go to be 9 feet tall. It's just terribly complex, very difficult to work through, and there's a lot of talk about old flat taxes and things like that, and that's going to get serious consideration. You know, last year the IRS issued rules requiring farmers and ranchers to change the way the account for repairs and maintenance and supplies. new rules force the capitalization of these costs, meaning that they have to depreciate over a number of years. That's very different from the old rule, which allowed the cost to be deducted right away. We have joined and tried to help lead some farm state senators to raise the issue of the IRS. They very begrudgingly released new rules to EAVs, the tax filing, and the reporting burdens of farmers, obviously the 179 expensing provision that was included in the tax extender, we have to protect that. Comprehensive tax reform, we are divided up into five working groups. I'm on the business and international working group. We are meeting in a bipartisan effort, just attended the meeting yesterday, one on business and one on international. The idea is at the end of the month that we take the consensus, if we can reach consensus. and put that into a comprehensive bill. Now, always before, Harry Reid has said the cost of that in moving it forward was a trillion dollars. We would always ask what the trillion dollars would be spent for, and they would always come up with some kind of a program, and we would always say, well, wait a minute, that's also involved revenue enhancement, that's all taxes, and we don't want to do that. So I don't know if we finally get down to that or not. There's another school of thought, Jeff, and that would be to take things that we know that we could do, pretty much what's on the tax extenders. You get into health care with regards to repealing the medical device tax. Make sure we have the 179 expensing. I could go down the list. These are things we can do that has bipartisan support. Eventually, if we can't get to a comprehensive tax reform, we could do that.

turn_text: Senator, you have experience in the Intelligence Committee and also in agriculture. And there are many who would like to see more normalized trade with Cuba. President's already taken action and there is a legislation that would eliminate the embargo. What is the pro and the con of working with our communist neighbors to the south?

Well, we were going to have a hearing and learn from the administration precisely what our trade posture will be with Cuba as opposed to simply saying we're going to trade with Cuba. We obviously need to expand our trade with that country if we possibly can. I don't know of any farm organization or commodity. group that is opposed to that, off a lot of people that are for it. We had a scheduling conflict with some of the witnesses. We're going to reschedule the hearing for next month, and we hope to learn from the administration precisely what we're talking about. I think we have to be realistic in this. I have been to Cuba with a trade mission some years ago. I went on my own with Max Baucus to talk to Fidel. Obviously, it is a brother, Ray Olve, who is in charge now. They haven't changed. It's a communist regime. We would always get into a trade talk and we would be able to sell whatever we were trying to sell, whether it's the products to schools and the hospitals and restaurants. And then all the rest of it, we ended up with a state-owned enterprise or a state enterprise, and you sort of hit a brick wall. And then you wondered about extending our export programs to a regime that still hasn't changed much, to say the least. And so those questions have to be answered, it seems to me. On the whole, let's have the hearing, and let's hear the projectors. I think this is one of those issues that the President has a bucket list with regards to his legacy, and he just simply pulled that out and said, well, we're going to trade with Cuba. And so the opportunities will be in the details and that's why we'll have the hearing.
